T1: Home bakers and coffee brewers pay a premium for a scale whose stated accuracy they can verify, because small weight errors visibly change results. A precision brand that certifies accuracy and offers calibration can capture that premium at the consumer price point. Who benefits: Serious home bakers, home coffee brewers and small artisan producers who currently accept scales with unspecified accuracy. Why behaviour changes: They learn that most consumer scales do not state accuracy, and that errors of a few grams matter for their process, so they will pay more for a specified and verifiable tolerance. How value is captured: Premium-priced consumer hardware with a published accuracy specification, sold through online and specialist retail, plus a low-cost calibration certificate or service. Assumptions: Buyers in these niches care about accuracy enough to pay more; A consumer price premium is achievable without the direct sales force; Mettler's existing calibration and certification capability can be offered at low cost per unit. Predictions: Among home bakers shown an accuracy-specified scale and an unspecified one at the same price, a measurable share chooses the specified one; Willingness to pay rises when a tolerance number and certificate are shown; Reviews of precision-specified consumer scales mention accuracy more often than reviews of standard scales.

T2: Consumers do not pay for measurement accuracy at home. The consumer scale market is price-driven and most buyers accept a few grams of error. A direct-sales precision company cannot reach consumer price points profitably, so the only viable way to capture consumer value is to license the technology or brand to an existing consumer scale maker, not to build its own consumer line. Who benefits: Existing consumer scale brands and retailers, who already own the mass channel and can sell at low prices; Mettler would earn a royalty or licence fee. Why behaviour changes: Mass retailers and consumer brands buy cheap, mainstream scales on price and convenience; a precision spec adds cost without a purchase reason, so buyers do not switch for accuracy. How value is captured: Licence or co-brand fees, or component supply of load cells and electronics, paid by a consumer brand that owns distribution and marketing. Assumptions: Mass consumer buyers rarely check or demand a stated accuracy figure; Consumer scale brands would pay a licence fee for a precision brand or technology; Mettler's direct-sales cost base cannot match retail price points. Predictions: Most consumer scales in mainstream retail do not state an accuracy tolerance; Price is the main ranking factor in mainstream consumer scale reviews, not accuracy; Consumer scale makers' licensing or component deals with precision instrument firms are rare or absent in public records.

T1 contradicts, from mettler-atk-tolerance (market_fact): "A range of ±3 grams is common and acceptable for most cooking, and most consumer-level scales don't specify their accuracy range.". Does not show: It is one US tester's view of cooking scales. It does not measure whether serious home bakers or coffee brewers would pay more for a specified tolerance, and the first half of the quote (that most cooking tolerates ±3 g) cuts against T1's premium claim, while the second half (accuracy often unspecified) only shows a gap in supply, not demand..

T2 supports, from mettler-ar25-ohaus (company_assertion): "Ohaus-branded products target markets, such as the educational market, in which customers are interested in lower cost, a more limited set of features, and less comprehensive support and service.". Does not show: This is the company's own description of a lower-cost brand for educational buyers in the Americas. It does not show that consumer buyers reject precision, that licensing is possible, or what Ohaus earns. It also shows Mettler already sells a low-cost line through another channel, which weakens T2's claim that a precision firm cannot reach low price points at all..
Looked for evidence against T2: "premium consumer kitchen scale accuracy specification sold at higher price"; found mettler-atk-tolerance, mettler-ar25-price-premium, mettler-ar25-channels.

T2 neutral, from mettler-ar25-price-premium (company_assertion): "Our dedication to continuously bringing innovations to market helps increase our value proposition, stimulate replacement demand, gain market share, and support our price premiums in the marketplace.". Does not show: This is the company's own claim about its core professional markets, with no figures and no consumer segment. It does not show that consumers pay for precision, nor does it refute T2. It is neutral on both T1 and T2..

Test "Specified-tolerance preference test with home bakers and coffee brewers" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice test with a landing page and paid-social recruitment. Respondents see two identical-looking consumer scales at different price points: one with a stated tolerance and a calibration certificate, one with no stated tolerance. Measure choice share, and offer a real pre-order option on the specified scale at the end. Proposed, not run.. Sample: Proposed: about 600 adults who bake or brew coffee at home at least weekly, recruited in two markets (for example the UK and Germany), with a cell of about 300 per arm. Measure: Share choosing the specified-tolerance scale at each price premium (for example +0%, +20%, +40% over the unspecified scale); pre-order conversion on the specified scale. Predictions: T1: A measurable share, roughly 25% or more, chooses the specified-tolerance scale even at a +20% premium, and conversion holds up when the tolerance figure and certificate are shown; T2: Choice share for the specified scale collapses to under 10% once any premium is shown; price dominates and the tolerance figure adds little. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 25% choose the specified scale at +20% and pre-order conversion is at least 3% of visitors, continue to a consumer prototype test under T1. If under 10% choose it at +20%, drop the consumer line and examine licensing under T2. Between 10% and 25%, treat as inconclusive and do not invest beyond the test.. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not invest in a Mettler-branded consumer hardware line now. Keep the no-expansion option as the default. Keep the specified-tolerance preference test (X1, proposed) as a low-cost check of T1 before any consumer product spend, and look at licensing or component supply to existing consumer scale makers as the more plausible route to consumer value. Nothing I read shows that Mettler sells to individual buyers directly; I could not establish its consumer reach from public sources. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: likely.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a Mettler-branded consumer hardware line now. Keep no expansion as the default. Test T1 cheaply before any consumer product spend, and treat licensing or component supply to existing consumer scale makers as the more plausible consumer route, though it is untested. Target customer: No consumer segment is recommended yet. Home bakers and home coffee brewers are the candidate niche to test under T1. Consumer scale makers are the potential licensing partners under T2.. Value proposition: Not established. Under T1, a published, verifiable accuracy tolerance with a calibration certificate, at a premium. Under T2, licence or component revenue from a consumer brand that owns the mass channel.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Do not commit product spend. If the company wants evidence, run the proposed specified-tolerance preference test (X1, about 12,000 EUR and 8 weeks, both figures my estimates, not yet run). Its decision rule: at least 25% choosing the specified scale at a +20% premium and at least 3% pre-order conversion supports T1; under 10% supports T2. Separately, establish from non-public or company sources whether Mettler already sells to individual buyers through Ohaus, distributors or online.. Uncertainty: High. The evidence is thin: one US test-kitchen publication (ATK, whose date shows as 2026-10-07, later than the annual report date, which I could not reconcile), two company claims about professional and educational markets, and no consumer sales data. I found nothing that contradicts T2 after one challenge search, but that search was narrow. I could not find any evidence of consumer willingness to pay for stated accuracy. Mettler's contracts, licence terms and consumer sales figures are not public. Test figures are my proposals, not observations.. Would change if: The X1 test shows at least 25% choosing a specified-tolerance scale at a +20% premium, which would favour T1; Evidence that home bakers or coffee brewers publicly demand stated tolerances or pay more for them; Public evidence that Mettler already sells consumer scales directly or through retail, which would change the reach baseline; Evidence that consumer scale makers have no interest in licence or component deals with precision firms, which would weaken the T2 route; A published consumer-facing accuracy standard or retailer requirement that raises the value of stated tolerance. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: likely.

T1: Individual buyers of household gloves choose on price and habit, not on a product difference, so a differentiated consumer glove cannot earn a premium that covers consumer marketing costs. Ansell's consumer business was therefore better run by a specialist consumer marketer. Who benefits: Consumers, who buy at commodity prices; and a specialist consumer brand owner who controls marketing and retail shelf space. Why behaviour changes: Consumers switch brands only when a visible, understood benefit justifies the price gap. For household gloves the benefit (protection from chemicals, fit) is hard to see at shelf, so purchase follows price and habit.. How value is captured: A manufacturer captures value only if it owns the brand and consumer marketing. Where it does not, the brand owner keeps most of the premium, so Ansell's share is limited to supply margin.. Assumptions: Household glove purchase is driven mainly by price and brand habit; Consumer marketing and retail distribution are the scarce capabilities, not glove manufacturing; A differentiated feature would be copied quickly by rivals. Predictions: Price premiums for a feature-led glove over a standard glove in retail will be small or absent; Consumer brands that own marketing will show higher margins than private-label or contract suppliers; A pilot with a feature claim will show no lift in purchase rate at equal price.

T2: Individual buyers with a specific sensitivity need, such as sensitive skin or latex allergy, will pay a premium for gloves whose safety is backed by medical-grade testing. A company with Ansell's healthcare credibility can capture that premium where generalist household brands cannot, but only in a narrow need-led niche rather than general household cleaning. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Safety Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners and small business owners. Participants view a product description of a new floor-cleaning tool (e.g., a compact scrubber) and are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) convenience and sustainability messaging (e.g., "Faster cleaning, less water waste, perfect for small spaces"); (B) safety and child-safe messaging (e.g., "Child-safe design, slip-resistant surface, trusted for families"). After viewing the description, participants indicate their willingness to pay a premium (willingness-to-pay) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from a panel of homeowners and small business owners in the United States and Western Europe.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each condition. Secondary measure: purchase intent (likelihood to buy on a 7-point scale).. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the convenience/sustainability condition compared to the safety condition.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the safety condition compared to the convenience condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the convenience condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the safety condition, conclude that T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the safety condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the convenience condition, conclude that T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Hach Company should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific water-quality use case (for example home drinking water testing), beyond its existing utility and industrial instruments, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The objective is to protect the core business while testing whether a consumer or near-consumer segment creates enough value to justify the cost.. Constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Financial and contractual detail (segment revenue, consumer sales, channel agreements) may not be public and must be flagged as unknown; Test budget of EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining; must establish what Hach already sells to individual buyers before theorising; Must not assume existing consumer reach; must verify it; Brand, regulatory (drinking water and reagent safety) and channel constraints may limit consumer entry. Alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the utility and industrial focus and change nothing for consumers; B. Product redesign: simplify or ruggedise an existing test kit for non-expert users, sold through existing channels; C. Different route to buyers: sell existing test kits or reagents to consumers via retail, e-commerce or partners such as well-water or pool service channels; D. Different customer group: serve small commercial or institutional buyers (restaurants, schools, small food producers, pool operators) rather than households; E. Partnership or licensing: let a home water-treatment or appliance brand integrate Hach test technology, so Hach captures value without owning consumer distribution; F. Subscription or testing-as-a-service layer paired with existing instruments for a niche user group.
Searched for "Hach consumer home water test kit"; found hach-distribution-consumers, hach-sfpuc-availability, hach-sfpuc-reliability.

T1: Households buy home water test kits mainly to reassure themselves about distribution-system risks (lead, copper, bacteria) that they cannot see, so a simple, trusted kit sold at retail or online captures demand that utilities and industrial instruments do not reach. Who benefits: Households with concern about tap water quality, especially in older buildings or after a local incident; Hach would benefit by selling a consumer-grade kit under its brand.. Why behaviour changes: Utilities meet regulatory standards at the plant, but the company's own page says water 'can come in contact with various components within the distribution system that potentially alter the quality' before it reaches consumers. That gap in visibility gives households a reason to test at the tap.. How value is captured: Hach sells kits and reagents through retail or e-commerce, earning margin on repeat consumables (reagent refills) and possibly a brand premium over generic kits sold by hardware stores.. Assumptions: Consumer concern about tap water is strong enough to drive repeat purchases, not one-off curiosity; Kits sold to consumers can deliver results that households find credible and actionable; Hach's brand carries enough trust in consumer channels to command a premium over existing kits; Consumer kits can be made without undermining the company's utility and industrial reputation. Predictions: Purchases concentrate among households with known distribution-system concerns (old pipes, recent boil notices, lead-service lines); Repeat purchase of reagents exceeds one-off kit purchase within 12 months; Willingness to pay for a branded kit rises when the result is framed as an alert about distribution-system risk rather than general quality; Sales spike after publicised local water-quality incidents and decay afterwards.

T2: Households do not trust home test kits as a final answer, so they treat kits only as a screening step and pay for certified laboratory confirmation. The value sits in the confirmatory testing service and the instruments behind it, not in the kit, so a consumer proposition should route buyers to accredited labs or partners rather than sell kits alone. Who benefits: Households who need a reliable answer about their water, and accredited laboratories or partners that run confirmatory tests; Hach benefits if it supplies the instruments, reagents or certified methods behind those labs.. Why behaviour changes: The public utility itself tells consumers that a kit result 'should be considered an initial step, not a final result' and should be confirmed by a laboratory with certified methods. Once a kit flags a problem, the buyer needs a trusted answer, and the kit alone cannot provide it, so the buyer pays for lab confirmation.. How value is captured: Hach earns revenue by supplying instruments, reagents and certified methods to laboratories or a sample-collection and mail-in service, rather than by selling the kit itself to households. It could also license its certified methods to partner labs.. Assumptions: Consumers will pay for lab confirmation after a screening result that looks alarming; Accredited labs or mail-in services can be run at a price households accept; Hach's instruments and reagents are the cost-effective route for the confirmatory tests; Kit makers and hardware retailers will not capture the confirmation step themselves. Predictions: Households that receive an alarming kit result will order confirmatory lab tests at a meaningful rate, compared with those who receive a clean result; Revenue per household is higher for confirmation services than for kit sales alone; Uptake of confirmatory tests depends on price and turnaround time more than on kit brand; Utilities and state agencies that promote kit screening also promote certified lab follow-up, which increases lab demand.

T1 supports, from hach-distribution-consumers (company_assertion): "Once treated water leaves the plant, it can come in contact with various components within the distribution system that potentially alter the quality of the water before it reaches consumers.". Does not show: This is Hach's own marketing claim. It does not show that households are worried about distribution-system risk, that they would buy a kit to check it, or how large that demand is. It also gives no date or geography..

T2 supports, from hach-sfpuc-reliability (regulation): "Home test kit results should be considered an initial step, not a final result. A poor water quality result by a kit should be confirmed with follow-up analyses by a laboratory that uses state-of-the-art instruments, certified methods, and quality control measures to ensure accuracy and reliability.". Does not show: This is a San Francisco utility's guidance, not a measurement of how many households pay for lab confirmation or what they would pay. It does not show that confirmatory lab demand is large, that Hach supplies those labs, or that households will act on an alarming result..

Looked for evidence against T2: "households do not pay for lab confirmation of home test kit results; kit results are sufficient; home test kits used without follow-up"; found hach-sfpuc-reliability, hach-pfas-kit-price, hach-sfpuc-availability.

T2 contradicts, from hach-pfas-kit-price (market_fact): "Cyclopure, an Illinois-based company, sells water test kits at $79 apiece — a more cost-effective but lesser-known alternative that scientists and local organizations have pointed to for more frequent monitoring.". Does not show: This is one competitor's kit in one town, a PFAS-specific case reported by a newspaper. It does not show that households pay for lab confirmation, that kits are reliable enough to be final, or what share of demand goes to kits versus labs. It is not Hach data..

Test "Tap-test screening with confirmation offer (proposed, not run)" between T1; T2. Method: Landing-page and paid-search test in one or two metro areas with older housing stock. Households searching for tap water testing see an offer for a home kit with an option to add an accredited lab confirmation, or a kit-only offer, at randomised prices. Measure click-through, pre-orders and confirmation add-on take-up. No product is shipped if the pre-order is not converted; deposits are refunded.. Sample: Proposed: roughly 3,000 to 5,000 ad impressions per arm across two metros over 8 weeks; target at least 150 completed pre-orders in total (estimated, to give usable take-up rates). Measure: Kit-only pre-order rate per 100 clicks; share of kit buyers who add lab confirmation at checkout; repeat-order intent after a simulated alarming result (survey item); price sensitivity across randomised price points. Predictions: T1: Kit-only pre-order rate is substantial and rises when the offer is framed around distribution-system risk (lead, copper, bacteria); repeat-order intent is high; confirmation add-on take-up is low because the kit is trusted enough to act on.; T2: Kit-only pre-order rate is lower than the confirmation-bundle rate per click; a large share of kit buyers add lab confirmation at checkout, and take-up of the add-on rises when the kit result is framed as 'initial screen'.. Decision rule: Proceed to a consumer kit pilot (T1 path) only if kit-only pre-orders reach at least 2 per 100 clicks AND fewer than 15% of buyers add confirmation AND survey repeat-intent is at least 30%. Pursue the confirmation or partner-lab route (T2 path) if confirmation add-on take-up is at least 25% of kit buyers and the bundle converts at least 1.5 times the kit-only rate. Otherwise do not invest beyond the test; keep the utility and industrial focus. Thresholds are analyst proposals, not company figures.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not commit to a consumer kit business now. Hach's existing utility and industrial instruments are the core. If anything consumer-facing is pursued, test a confirmation-led route (accredited lab or partner-lab service, with Hach supplying instruments, reagents or methods) before building a kit product. The 20,000 EUR, 10-week test X1 is a proposal only and has not been run. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep Hach focused on its utility and industrial instruments. If revisited, run a small, cheap demand test before any product investment. The most promising consumer-adjacent route in the evidence is confirmation-led testing (accredited-lab or partner-lab service, with Hach supplying instruments, reagents or certified methods), not a branded household kit. Target customer: No consumer target is justified yet. If tested, the candidate is households with a specific distribution-system worry (older buildings, lead-service lines, a recent boil notice) who need a result they can act on.. Value proposition: Not established. The only candidate supported by the sources is reliable certified confirmation of a screening result, which the San Francisco utility's guidance says is needed. Whether households will pay for it is untested.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Do not spend the 20,000 EUR yet. If management wants an answer, run proposed test X1 (landing-page and pre-order test, two metros, about 10 weeks, EUR 18,000; all parameters analyst-proposed) to separate kit-led demand (T1) from confirmation-led demand (T2). First, establish from internal records how much Hach already sells to individual buyers.. Uncertainty: High. Hach's consumer sales, channel agreements and segment revenue were not findable in public sources. Evidence is thin: one Hach marketing page (company claim), two San Francisco utility pages (kits widely sold; results should be lab-confirmed), and one report on a competitor's $79 PFAS kit. None measures household demand, willingness to pay or repeat purchase. Nothing shows Hach sells consumer kits. X1 is unrun; its thresholds are my estimates.. Would change if: Internal data show Hach already sells meaningful volume to individual buyers through a channel I did not find; X1 shows kit-only pre-orders at or above 2 per 100 clicks, confirmation add-on below 15% and repeat intent at or above 30% (supports T1); X1 shows at least 25% of kit buyers taking confirmation and a bundle converting at least 1.5 times the kit-only rate (supports T2); Accredited labs or utilities already fill the confirmation role cheaply, leaving little room for Hach; A large consumer kit market with strong brands already exists, making entry costly without a clear differentiator; A major local water-quality incident creating sustained household demand for testing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).; 2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.; 4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).; 5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand..

T1: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation products if they perceive them as a reliable, professional-grade solution that simplifies the installation process, because they value ease of use and confidence in the product's performance. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking energy efficiency upgrades without major renovations.. Why behaviour changes: They are willing to pay a premium for a product that is marketed as a "DIY" solution but delivered by professionals, reducing installation risk and time.. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and potential retail partnerships that increase brand visibility.. Assumptions: Consumers trust professional-grade insulation over generic DIY products.; Marketing can effectively communicate the "DIY" yet professional delivery promise.; Kingspan can reach homeowners through existing channels (e.g., B&Q, online).. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show higher purchase intent for Kingspan when presented with a "DIY" yet professional delivery message compared to a generic DIY brand.; Sales of Kingspan's consumer-facing products would increase in regions where DIY insulation is already popular.; Retail partnerships would generate higher average transaction value than selling directly..

T2: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a cost-effective, government‑funded upgrade, because they are motivated by financial incentives and energy‑bill savings. Who benefits: Homeowners of older homes (pre‑2011) who qualify for energy‑efficiency grants and are motivated by reducing long‑term energy costs.. Why behaviour changes: They are willing to invest in insulation when the upfront cost is offset by a refundable grant and lower annual heating bills, making the purchase feel like a financial return rather than a discretionary purchase.. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value through partnerships with government grant schemes, bundled pricing that includes grant eligibility, and data on grant recipients to identify high‑potential segments.. Assumptions: Government grant schemes are accessible and actively promoted to homeowners.; Kingspan can integrate grant eligibility into its product offering without significant redesign.; Homeowners are aware of and trust the grant process.. Predictions: A test offering a grant‑eligible Kingspan kit would show higher conversion rates among homeowners who have received or are eligible for a grant.; Sales would be concentrated in regions with higher grant participation rates.; The average transaction value would be higher when the kit includes a grant application guide..

Test "DIY vs Grant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A sees a "DIY" yet professional-grade product description emphasizing ease of installation and confidence in performance; Condition B sees a grant‑eligible product description emphasizing a refundable grant and energy‑bill savings. Both conditions include a purchase decision question with a stated price tolerance.. Sample: 500 UK homeowners (250 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, home ownership, and energy‑efficiency interest.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum price willing to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and higher average price willingness than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and higher average price willingness than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition B purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition A purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Kingspan's insulation as a professional‑grade, "DIY‑yet‑professional‑delivered" solution, leveraging existing direct‑to‑consumer channels (website, online ordering) and retail partnerships (e.g., B&Q). This aligns with evidence of direct‑to‑consumer sales and the company’s "DIY" marketing claims, while addressing the contradiction that professional‑grade‑ Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer motivation, trust, or purchase intent for Kingspan's insulation products. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

Test "Digital vs. Standalone Home CPR Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a safety-focused home CPR message (e.g., "Be prepared to save a life with home CPR training.") and Group B sees a convenience-focused home CPR message (e.g., "Learn CPR in 20 minutes with our portable kit."). Both groups view a product description of Laerdal’s home CPR kit and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 500 health-conscious adults recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Primary measure: average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale). Secondary measure: share of participants indicating intent to purchase each message.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, because the safety message aligns with the perceived risk of cardiac arrest and the desire to be prepared.; T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with the desire for easy, data-backed wellness solutions.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the safety message is at least 1.5 times the average WTP for the convenience message (i.e., WTP_safety ≥ 1.5 × WTP_convenience), proceed to develop a safety-focused consumer proposition. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Convenience Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult consumers in Germany and Switzerland, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this machine?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "How much would you pay more than a comparable entry-level machine?" (WTP in euros). 3) Messaging preference: "Which attribute matters more to you?" (Quality vs Convenience).. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will generate at least 15% higher purchase intent and higher WTP than convenience messaging.; T2: Convenience messaging will generate at least 15% higher purchase intent and higher WTP than premium messaging.. Decision rule: If premium messaging yields purchase intent at least 15% higher than convenience messaging AND WTP difference is at least €10, proceed with a premium consumer proposition. If convenience messaging yields purchase intent at least 15% higher AND WTP difference is at least €10, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Home CPR Kit Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product concepts: (1) premium-priced home CPR kit (e.g., Laerdal Anytime) marketed as a private, convenient solution for family training; (2) low-cost, bulk B2B training kit marketed as a professional solution. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each kit and cite reasons (privacy/convenience vs cost/need).. Sample: 400 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect U.S. households. Randomly assigned to see either the premium-priced kit or the low-cost kit.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason (open-ended) for choosing each kit.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the premium-priced kit and higher frequency of citing privacy/convenience as the primary reason.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the low-cost kit and higher frequency of citing cost/need as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the premium-priced kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and privacy/convenience reasons ≥ 30% of respondents, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training. If the low-cost kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and cost/need reasons ≥ 30%, consider a low‑cost consumer offering. If neither meets threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Belimo's value in residential heating control is captured through installers and contractors, not individual buyers. Homeowners and landlords adopt zone control when a qualified installer recommends and fits it, so the installer channel Belimo already serves is the route to demand. Who benefits: HVAC installers and controls contractors, who earn installation margin and avoid callbacks; then homeowners and landlords who get working zone control.. Why behaviour changes: Installers already sell and fit commercial and light-commercial controls. A product that fits their workflow, has training behind it, and reduces commissioning failures gives them a reason to recommend it to residential customers.. How value is captured: Belimo sells components through distributors and installer networks, using the technical support and HVAC professional training its annual report describes, rather than building a consumer brand.. Assumptions: Installers would bring residential zone-control jobs to Belimo-based products if the product is simple to fit; Residential retrofit jobs run through contractors who already buy from the manufacturer's channel; Installer margin is large enough to change their recommendation. Predictions: In a pilot with installers, quote and attachment rates for residential zone control exceed those for direct-to-consumer ads; Installers report fewer commissioning callbacks with a residential-specific kit than with a generic valve; Consumer willingness to pay is lower when no installer recommends the product.

T2: Homeowners buy heating control directly from the brand when they see the energy saving themselves, as tado and Nest did. A consumer-branded product sold online can therefore capture value that installer channels do not reach. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who want lower heating bills and control from an app, and the brand that owns the customer relationship and the subscription or repeat revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Heating bills are visible and frequent, so a clear saving claim and an app make the purchase feel like a comfort and cost decision rather than a building-services job.. How value is captured: Belimo would sell a retail or online product and keep the margin that installers and distributors take in the B2B channel.. Assumptions: Homeowners can install or accept a self-fit product without a contractor; Energy saving claims are credible enough to persuade buyers without installer endorsement; Consumer acquisition cost is low enough to make online sales profitable. Predictions: A direct-to-consumer ad test converts at a rate that makes customer acquisition cost lower than the gross margin per unit; Buyers who pay themselves show higher app engagement than buyers who were installer-fitted; Consumer revenue is volatile, so sustained sales need repeat or subscription income.

Test "Installer-referral versus direct-online pilot for residential zone control" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm pilot in one metro area with one residential zone-control kit (existing hardware, no new product). Arm A: sell through 10 to 15 installers who fit the kit and quote homeowners and landlords. Arm B: run online paid search and social ads with a self-fit or installer-finder CTA, sending buyers to the same kit. Track quotes, sales and callbacks for 8 weeks after a 2-week setup.. Sample: Proposed: 10 to 15 installers and about 1,500 ad-driven visitors split over 8 weeks. Budget and sample sizes are estimates for this exercise.. Measure: Quote-to-sale conversion per arm; cost per acquired customer per arm; installer-reported callbacks per 10 installs; share of ad buyers who request an installer.. Predictions: T1: Arm A converts quotes to sales at a higher rate than Arm B, with fewer callbacks, and a meaningful share of Arm B buyers asks for an installer, showing demand routes through installers.; T2: Arm B cost per acquired customer falls below gross margin per unit, and few Arm B buyers ask for an installer, showing homeowners buy direct.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: favour T2 only if Arm B cost per customer is below 60 percent of unit gross margin and under 20 percent of Arm B buyers request an installer. Favour T1 if Arm A quote-to-sale conversion is at least 1.5 times Arm B and Arm A callbacks are at most half of the national baseline. Otherwise keep both theories open.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a consumer brand yet. If Belimo pursues residential demand at all, test it first through its existing installer and contractor channel with a residential zone-control kit, using the 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot as a gate. No evidence I read shows Belimo sells to individual buyers today; its public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels only. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not start a consumer brand now. Belimo's public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels, and I found no evidence that it sells to individual buyers today. If management wants residential demand, test it first through the installer channel with a residential zone-control kit, gated by a 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot. The pilot is a proposal and has not been run. Target customer: Installers and controls contractors serving residential and small-landlord retrofits (provisional, untested). Direct homeowners are a secondary segment to test, not a target yet.. Value proposition: A residential-fit zone-control kit that installers can fit and commission with fewer callbacks, backed by the technical support and training Belimo already gives HVAC professionals. Unproven.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed two-arm pilot (X1), installer-referral arm versus direct-online arm, with the decision rule as proposed. First confirm how installers in the target market are paid and recruited, and check the company's own residential sales data, which is not public.. Uncertainty: High. Belimo's own residential sales, channel mix, margins, installer economics and acquisition costs are not public. The Belimo sources are company self-descriptions. Consumer comparisons (tado, Nest, Airthings, Resideo) are other companies' results and do not show Belimo could replicate them. Airthings reported 2025 consumer revenue down 20% while its professional segment grew, which weakens the consumer case. The pilot figures are my estimates.. Would change if: Belimo's own data or disclosures show meaningful existing residential or direct sales; The pilot shows Arm B cost per customer below 60 percent of unit gross margin, with under 20 percent of buyers asking for an installer, which would favour T2; Installers show no interest or margin at residential job sizes, weakening T1; Thermostat or smart-home platforms want valves or actuators that solve system compatibility, pointing to licensing; Independent data show European homeowners buy zone control without installers at scale. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Alternatives: A. No expansion: keep focus on trade, food and industry B2B instruments; B. Consumer or prosumer product line (e.g. homeowner-grade measuring tools) sold via retail or online; C. Product redesign of existing trade instruments to be easier for semi-professional or individual users; D. T1: Homeowners buy indoor-climate measuring devices when a trusted trade professional recommends them as part of a service visit, so the value sits with the installer channel, not with a direct consumer product. Who benefits: Heating and ventilation installers and service firms (who sell checks and remedies); homeowners who get a verified reading; Testo if it supplies the trade-grade meter and app that the installer uses and lends or resells to customers.. Why behaviour changes: A homeowner who is unsure whether a problem (humidity, CO2, mould, heating performance) is real is more likely to act on a reading taken by a professional they already trust than on a cheap device bought online whose accuracy they cannot judge.. How value is captured: Testo sells professional probes and an app licence through installers, plus possibly a rental or per-visit fee or a homeowner app tier; the margin comes from the installer's willingness to pay for accuracy and documentation.. Assumptions: Homeowners distrust low-cost consumer meters for decisions with cost consequences; Installers already visit homes for heating or ventilation work and could use a measuring step as a sales tool; Testo's existing trade relationships reach these installers; Installers will pay for or recommend the device rather than treating it as a free add-on. Predictions: Installers who receive a Testo kit will report more homeowner follow-up work than installers who do not, in a matched pilot; Homeowners will pay more for a visit-based reading than for a self-use device of similar price; Demand will be concentrated in installers already active in ventilation or heat pump work, not spread across all homeowners.

T2: Individual buyers of measuring instruments are price-led and do-it-yourself oriented, so demand is episodic and driven by news or crises (for example the 2020 surge in CO2 traffic lights), and a precision brand captures little of it; the value of a consumer line would be short-lived and would rest on low-cost competitors. Who benefits: Consumers, who obtain cheap meters; low-cost and app-first competitors (for example Airthings, which reports selling more than 1.5m consumer devices) and retailers, who capture most margin; Testo would benefit only if it could price above these competitors.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers buy a meter when a visible event raises fear (a pandemic, a heating scare), and then pick the cheapest acceptable device; accuracy and trade credibility matter little to them, so a premium does not hold once the scare passes.. How value is captured: Value would come from volume sales through retail or online channels at low margin, which Testo would have to fund against established consumer brands; it is the reverse of the trade channel model in T1.. Assumptions: Consumer purchases follow news or crisis peaks rather than steady need; Price is the main purchase criterion for individual buyers of air-quality meters; Established consumer brands already hold distribution that a newcomer would have to buy into; A trade-grade brand does not command a visible premium with individuals. Predictions: Sales of consumer CO2 and air-quality meters will show peaks tied to news events and fall back afterwards; Price comparison sites will show most sales at the lowest-priced acceptable device, not the most accurate; A higher-priced, trade-grade device sold to consumers will sell far fewer units than a low-cost equivalent at the same retailer.

T1 contradicts, from testo-airthings-volume (company_assertion): "Airthings shipped more than 220,000 devices and has since inception sold more than 1.5m air quality devices to its customers". Does not show: Whether these consumers were advised by a professional, what share came through retail versus installers, or whether buyers distrust cheap meters. It is a company's own annual-report claim, not an independent measure of demand. It does show that a direct consumer channel can reach volume, which weakens T1's claim that installer recommendation is needed..

T2 supports, from testo-dhz-co2-demand (market_fact): "Aktuell werden CO2-Ampeln stark nachgefragt.". Does not show: Whether this demand peak lasted, how large it was, or whether it fell back afterwards. It is a single 2020 trade-press remark, and it does not compare price with accuracy or show that a premium fails. It supports only that demand for consumer CO2 devices was strong at one moment..

T2 neutral, from testo-airthings-decline (company_assertion): "revenues declined 22% in the Consumer segment". Does not show: The cause of the fall in demand. The company attributes it to inventory reduction and unit-economics changes, not to a demand peak ending, so it does not confirm that consumer demand is episodic. It also does not show channel share or price competition. It is the company's own annual-report figure..

Test "Installer-referred homeowner pilot versus consumer price test" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm field pilot in one region. Arm A: about 15 heating and ventilation installers each given a trade-grade probe and app, asked to offer a homeowner indoor-climate check during existing visits, with the homeowner paying a fixed fee for a documented reading. Arm B: a consumer-grade listing of the same probe at two price points on one online marketplace, with a 4-week window and a news-neutral period.. Sample: Proposed: 15 installers in Arm A, roughly 150 homeowner visits; Arm B: one listing at two prices for 4 weeks, observed sales and conversion.. Measure: Arm A: number of paid homeowner checks per installer, and follow-up repair or upgrade work booked within 4 weeks. Arm B: units sold per week at each price, and the share of sales at the lowest acceptable price.. Predictions: T1: Installers in Arm A book follow-up work and homeowners pay the fee; Arm B sells few units at the higher price and little difference between price points is needed for the installer channel to work.; T2: Arm B sales concentrate at the lowest price and fall away after a short window; Arm A shows low uptake because homeowners do not pay for a reading they could buy cheaply.. Decision rule: Proceed to a trade-led consumer proposition only if at least 40 percent of installers in Arm A complete paid checks and at least 1 in 3 checks leads to booked follow-up work within 4 weeks (proposed thresholds). Reject the consumer retail route if Arm B sells fewer than 50 units at the higher price in 4 weeks while the lowest-price listing sells more than three times as many (proposed threshold). Otherwise repeat with a larger installer sample.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a consumer product line now. Test whether installer-referred indoor-climate checks create paid demand, using the proposed pilot X1, before committing to any consumer channel. Confirm Testo's existing installer reach first. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not build a consumer product line now. Run the installer-referred pilot (X1) first. The evidence I found does not show that Testo sells to individual buyers at all, so first establish that baseline before committing money. Target customer: Heating and ventilation installers and service firms, with homeowners as the paying end of an installer-led indoor-climate check. Not a mass consumer segment yet.. Value proposition: A trade-grade measurement and documentation kit that installers can use during a home visit to give homeowners a verified reading, for a fee or as part of a service.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Confirm Testo's current installer and consumer reach from its own disclosures, then run pilot X1 (proposed: about 15 installers, about 150 homeowner visits, roughly EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks; all figures estimated). Proceed only if the proposed thresholds are met.. Uncertainty: High. I found no source on Testo's existing consumer sales, pricing, channel mix or margins; these may be non-public. T1 is thinly supported: the Smart Probes brochure is a company claim about trade customers and says nothing about homeowners. Airthings' annual report shows a direct consumer channel can reach volume, which weakens T1. Airthings consumer revenue fell 22% in 2025 while sell-through grew, so demand looks volatile. T2 rests on one 2020 trade-press remark. Both theories are untested and search coverage was partial.. Would change if: Testo's own disclosures show a sizeable existing consumer or homeowner-sales business; The pilot shows installers will not pay for or promote a homeowner reading, which would reject T1 and point to no expansion; Consumer listing data show sales concentrated at the lowest price and falling after news peaks, which would support T2; Independent data show stable, non-episodic demand for homeowner measurement that a trade-grade brand can price above low-cost rivals; Airthings' sell-through growth proves to be channel-stuffing or reverses in later reporting. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: Hoshizaki Alliance is a group of independent companies that manufacture and market products for the food service industry, including ice machines, refrigerators, freezers, prep tables, display cases, and dispensers. Its brands include Hoshizaki America Inc., Lancer Worldwide, Jackson Warewashing Systems, Fogel Group and Hoshizaki Macom.

In overseas markets, Although the impact of macroeconomic trends and the competitive environment will remain severe, demand is expected to remain firm, particularly for key products (ice machines, refrigerators, and dispensers).

Commercial buyers are differentiating between high-output fleet equipment and compact point-of-service units, while residential consumers are entering the category through accessible countertop formats.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Hoshizaki should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is to find a consumer-facing offer that earns a return without damaging the core commercial franchise.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; company has not asked, has not been contacted, and its intentions are unknown.; Financial and contractual detail (distributor terms, direct-channel margins, consumer sales share) may not be public and must be flagged as unknown.; Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.; 7 searches remaining; each claim presented as observed must come from a read source.; Must find out how far Hoshizaki already reaches individual buyers before assuming it does not.. Alternatives: A. No expansion: keep commercial focus, serve consumers only indirectly through existing channels and dealers.; B. Product redesign: a compact or home-scale ice/refrigeration product sold through existing dealers to households.; C. Different route to buyers: an online or retail channel, or a service-subscription model for existing equipment owners, without a new product.; D. Different customer group: small hospitality venues, home-bar or hobby users, or offices, served with a packaged offer rather than a consumer brand.; E. Adjacent use case: refrigerated storage or beverage dispensing for a specific consumer segment, reusing existing components.; F. Partnership or licensing: let a consumer appliance brand carry a Hoshizaki-engineered component or technology, capturing value without consumer marketing..
Searched for "Hoshizaki consumer products household refrigerator ice maker"; found hoshizaki-japan-fridge-icemakers, hoshizaki-alliance-portfolio, hoshizaki-fy2025-outlook.

T1: Japanese households value automatic ice making as a feature of premium refrigerators. Hoshizaki could capture value by supplying compact ice-making modules to refrigerator makers, rather than selling a consumer-branded product, because the buyer chooses the fridge for its features and the ice maker is a component. Who benefits: Refrigerator makers (who gain a feature) and Hoshizaki (who sells a component into an existing commercial engineering base without consumer marketing).. Why behaviour changes: Household buyers who already compare features on premium fridges (cooling speed, humidity control, automatic ice) will pay more for a fridge that includes automatic ice, so the feature gets bundled rather than bought separately.. How value is captured: Component or OEM supply contracts at a per-unit price; no consumer brand, retail or after-sales cost to Hoshizaki.. Assumptions: Japanese consumers still rank automatic ice as a purchase factor (Renub lists it, but the source is a market-research summary with no date or method).; Refrigerator makers would accept an outside ice module and would not build their own.; Hoshizaki's commercial ice technology can be made small, quiet and cheap enough for a household fridge.; Refrigerator makers are willing to pay a per-unit price that covers Hoshizaki's engineering.. Predictions: Refrigerator makers in Japan who list automatic ice as a premium feature will be open to a supplier conversation (measurable by interview or RFQ response).; Sales of premium fridges with automatic ice grow faster than the wider fridge market (measurable from retail data).; Hoshizaki receives no or few inquiries from OEMs if the feature is weak to consumers..

T2: Hoshizaki's consumer value would come from its installed-base service relationship, not from the consumer sale. Households buying an ice or cold-drink appliance through a dealer or builder need after-sales maintenance, and a service contract on a residential unit captures recurring revenue that a one-off product sale does not. Who benefits: Households who want a reliable ice or cold-drink appliance without managing repairs, and Hoshizaki's service network, which is already built around maintenance of commercial units.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who are unsure about installing and maintaining an ice appliance at home will pay a recurring fee for guaranteed service, so they choose the brand offering service over a cheaper unit with no support.. How value is captured: Annual or per-visit service contracts on units sold through dealers and builders, with a margin on parts and call-outs, rather than on the appliance price alone.. Assumptions: Hoshizaki's direct sales and service network can extend to households at acceptable cost per visit.; Consumers will pay a recurring service fee for an appliance they consider low-risk.; Dealers or builders will route residential sales to Hoshizaki's service model.; The consumer segment is large enough that service fees cover the added network cost.. Predictions: Households offered a bundled service contract with an ice appliance take it up at a measurable rate (pilot sign-ups).; Consumers who buy with service cite repair fear or installation hassle as a reason, not ice quality.; Service revenue per residential unit stays positive after visit costs, measured in a pilot..

T1 supports, from hoshizaki-japan-fridge-icemakers (market_fact): "Modern Japanese consumers increasingly value features such as rapid cooling, humidity-controlled vegetable compartments, antibacterial interiors, automatic ice makers, and separate cooling zones for different food types.". Does not show: Renub Research is a commercial market-research summary with no date (accessed 2026-11-08 but publication date unknown) and no stated method or sample. It does not show that buyers would pay a premium for automatic ice, that refrigerator makers would buy an outside ice module, or that Hoshizaki can make one cheaply enough..

T2 neutral, from hoshizaki-alliance-portfolio (company_assertion): "Hoshizaki Alliance is a group of independent companies that manufacture and market products for the food service industry, including ice machines, refrigerators, freezers, prep tables, display cases, and dispensers.". Does not show: This is a trade-press description of the US Alliance group. It shows the group's stated market is food service, which is consistent with a commercial-service base, but it says nothing about whether a residential service network exists, what it costs per visit, or whether dealers would route household sales to it. It does not show Japanese direct-channel reach or the consumer share of sales..

Looked for evidence against T1: "refrigerator manufacturer ice maker supplier outsourcing consumer willingness to pay automatic ice feature"; found hoshizaki-japan-fridge-icemakers, hoshizaki-gmi-countertop, hoshizaki-imarc-countertop.

T1 contradicts, from hoshizaki-gmi-countertop (market_fact): "residential consumers are entering the category through accessible countertop formats.". Does not show: A global market-research overview with no stated method, no Japan data and no split between countertop units and built-in fridge modules. It does not show that consumers buy countertop units instead of fridges with built-in ice, only that a standalone residential entry route exists. It weakens T1's premise that ice is bundled into fridge purchases, but does not prove that OEM supply fails..

Test "Feature-bundle vs service-attach demand test (Japan, proposed)" between T1; T2. Method: Two-arm stated-preference and interest test. Arm A: a web survey plus conjoint choice of household fridges, with automatic ice as an attribute at several price points. Arm B: a refundable pre-order page for a countertop ice unit, with and without a bundled annual service plan at the same price. In parallel, structured interviews with refrigerator makers and appliance dealers in Japan to test OEM appetite for an outside ice module (T1), and dealer willingness to route residential sales to a service contract (T2).. Sample: Proposed: about 400 Japanese households who have bought or plan to buy a fridge in the next 12 months (online panel, quota-matched by region); 8 to 10 interviews with refrigerator makers and dealers. All sample sizes are estimates for this exercise.. Measure: Arm A: willingness to pay for automatic ice as a share of fridge choice and implied EUR premium. Arm B: pre-order conversion with vs without service plan, and service-plan take-up rate. Interviews: number of OEMs willing to hold a supplier discussion or RFQ.. Predictions: T1: Automatic ice carries a measurable premium in the conjoint and OEM interviews show several makers willing to open a supplier discussion; service plan adds little to pre-order conversion because ice is valued as a fridge feature.; T2: Service plan lifts pre-order conversion materially over no-plan, service take-up is high among buyers who cite repair or installation worry, and dealers will route residential sales to a service contract; OEM interest in ice modules is low or absent.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: favour T1 if at least 3 of 8 to 10 OEMs agree to a supplier discussion AND automatic ice shows at least a 10% premium in the conjoint. Favour T2 if the service-plan pre-order uplift is at least 15 percentage points over no-plan AND at least 3 dealers commit to routing. If neither threshold is met, or both are, treat the result as unresolved and do not commit more than the test budget. Thresholds are proposed, not validated.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Looked for evidence against T2: "appliance extended warranty service plan consumer uptake refusal residential ice maker maintenance"; found hoshizaki-gmi-countertop, hoshizaki-imarc-countertop, hoshizaki-profile.

Favours T2: Do not build a consumer product yet. The company's own profile describes its business as commercial kitchen appliances, and I found no source showing a household product or residential service offer. Of the two theories, T1 (bundled ice module sold to refrigerator makers) is weakened by the standalone countertop entry route in the GMI excerpt, and its key premise, that consumers value automatic ice enough to pay for it, rests on an undated market-research summary. T2 (service-attached residential sales) has no contrary evidence in my searches, but also no supporting evidence, so it is only worth testing. Run X1 before any decision, costing EUR 20,000 over 12 weeks as a proposed budget. If neither threshold is met, keep the commercial focus (alternative A). Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product or partnership now. Keep the commercial focus as the default (alternative A). Before any decision, run test X1 as a proposed EUR 20,000, 12-week check of two consumer routes: OEM ice-module supply (T1) and a service-attached residential offer (T2). Treat the thresholds as proposed, not validated. Target customer: Not yet determined. Candidate segments are Japanese households buying a fridge or countertop ice unit (T1 and T2 both point here), but no source establishes demand in this segment.. Value proposition: Unproven. A candidate is an automatic-ice module for refrigerator makers (T1) or a service contract on residential ice units (T2). Neither has evidence of willingness to pay.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Run test X1 (proposed): conjoint and pre-order test with about 400 Japanese households, plus 8 to 10 interviews with refrigerator makers and dealers. Ask Hoshizaki for its own residential sales and service data, which is not public.. Uncertainty: High. The company profile describes only commercial kitchen equipment, so no public source shows a household product or residential service. Renub's household claim is undated and has no stated method. The GMI excerpt suggests residential ice enters through standalone countertop units, which weakens T1. I found no source for Hoshizaki's direct-channel reach to individual buyers, consumer share of sales, distributor terms or margins; these are not public. Both theories are unverified.. Would change if: X1 shows at least 3 of 8 to 10 refrigerator makers agree to a supplier discussion and automatic ice shows at least a 10% conjoint premium: favour T1.; Service-plan pre-order uplift is at least 15 percentage points over no-plan and at least 3 dealers commit to routing sales: favour T2.; Internal company data shows an existing household customer base or residential service revenue, which would change the cost of entry.; Evidence that Japanese fridge buyers already get ice from standalone countertop units at low price would lower T1's value further.; Neither threshold met: drop the consumer proposition and keep alternative A.. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: uncertain.
